analysis.one_liner: Requires coal-fired power plants to cut their mercury emissions by at least 90 percent.
analysis.headline: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee held a hearing on the bill in May 2008 but never voted to advance it, and the bill died without ever reaching the Senate floor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to force the EPA to write rules cutting mercury emissions from coal- and oil-fired power plants by at least 90 percent. It was pitched as a fix after a federal court threw out the Bush administration's weaker mercury rule, which would have cut emissions only about half by 2020 and let plants trade pollution allowances. The bill cited evidence that mercury from coal plants ends up in fish and reaches roughly 630,000 children in the womb each year, harming attention, language, and memory, and said 90 percent cuts were achievable by 2010 with existing equipment like activated carbon injection and scrubbers. It never received a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who eat fish, anglers, and communities near contaminated waterways — the bill's own findings say mercury from coal plants concentrates in fish tissue and reaches about 630,000 children in the womb each year, risking lifelong attention, language, and memory problems. It would also benefit downwind states whose lakes receive mercury from power plants in other states, and companies that make the mercury-control equipment the bill's findings say is cheap and proven.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fish eaters, children, and fishing communities

how_it_helps.text: It directs EPA to write rules requiring at least a 90 percent reduction in mercury emissions from new and existing coal-fired power plants, the source of more than 45 percent of U.S. industrial mercury emissions.

It responds to the Bush administration's 2005 Clean Air Mercury Rule, which the bill's findings say would have cut mercury only about 50 percent by 2020 through a cap-and-trade program, and which a federal appeals court had struck down earlier in 2008.

The bill's findings state that about 630,000 children are born each year exposed to dangerous levels of methylmercury in the womb, at risk of neurological problems affecting attention, language, and memory, and that cutting emissions 90 percent was feasible by 2010 with already-available equipment.

analysis.who_pays: Coal- and oil-fired power plant operators, who would have had to install mercury controls such as activated carbon injection and fabric filters, and electricity customers, who would bear some of those costs through rates — though the bill's findings put the equipment cost at under $3 per kilowatt, a small addition to plant capital.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on coal-fired power plants, and utilities would have passed some of that spending through to electricity customers as higher rates, with effects largest in coal-reliant states.

The bill sets a rigid statutory requirement — not less than 90 percent for all units by regulation proposed within 180 days — leaving EPA little flexibility to tailor deadlines for plants with different coal types or existing scrubbers, which could make compliance more expensive than a performance-based rule.

Meeting the deadline would have pushed utilities to run existing scrubbers harder and add activated carbon injection, which can slightly degrade the capture of other pollutants like sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, and can add low levels of the injected carbon to ash disposal streams.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — a 90 percent cut in mercury from the largest industrial source, protecting an estimated 630,000 babies a year from in-womb exposure [S3] — was large, and the bill's own findings put the financial value in the billions annually [S3]. The main costs are real: coal plants would have had to install controls by 2010, with some of the spending passed through to electricity customers, and the mandate locked in one approach (activated carbon injection plus fabric filters) rather than letting performance rules find the cheapest path [S3]. On balance it was a focused, modest-cost public health measure with unusual bipartisan sponsorship, and the significant drawback is less its design than that it never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.mechanism: The committee held a hearing on it in May 2008 but never voted on it, and with the 110th Congress ending in January 2009 the bill expired without a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 14, 2008 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The committee's only action after referral was a hearing on May 13, 2008 (printed as S.Hrg. 110-1249); no markup, committee vote, or floor action followed.

Thirteen senators signed on in total — the sponsor plus 12 cosponsors split 7 Democrats, 4 Republicans, and 1 Independent — including original cosponsors from coal states such as Lamar Alexander of Tennessee and Judd Gregg of New Hampshire.
The bill was written to override the weaker approach left standing after the courts struck down the 2005 Clean Air Mercury Rule, which the findings say would have cut mercury only 50 percent by 2020.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-fired utilities and the coal industry were better off, because no binding 90 percent mercury reduction was ever imposed on them. Electricity customers avoided potential rate increases in the short term, while the expected public health benefits — fewer children exposed to methylmercury — were never delivered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-fired utilities; the cuts never happened

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill, held one hearing on May 13, 2008, and never scheduled a markup or committee vote on it; the bill left committee only by expiring at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Coal-fired electric utilities
against.what_they_did: Utilities and coal interests opposed mandatory maximum-achievable-control-technology standards for mercury, the same approach the Bush EPA had rejected in favor of a slower, weaker cap-and-trade rule.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsors were bipartisan — 12 cosponsors split 7 Democrats, 4 Republicans, and 1 Independent, including Republicans from coal and coal-adjacent states — so it died in committee without a party-line fight ever taking place.

industries.note: The bill forces these plants to cut mercury emissions by at least 90 percent, requiring them to install pollution controls such as activated carbon injection and fabric filters, with costs likely passed to electricity customers. Their interest runs against the public's because the mercury they emit accumulates in the fish people eat, especially harming children's development.

A strict 90 percent mercury mandate makes coal-fired generation more expensive relative to alternatives, weighing on demand for coal. The effect on miners and mining companies is indirect but negative.

Companies selling activated carbon injection systems and fabric filters would gain a large new customer base, since the bill's findings say the needed equipment costs less than $3 per kilowatt and was already proven at waste incinerators. This gain depends on the public mandate, not on public purchase.
